children.note: The first two years of school in Kenya's CBC, before Grade 1. Children learn mostly through play, songs, stories and talking. This map explains what they do, how teachers watch their progress, and simple ways parents can help at home.

children.note: Pre-primary is the start of school under the Competency Based Curriculum. It is the gentle first step into learning with other children.
Pre-primary has two years. PP1 comes first, then PP2, then the child moves to Grade 1.

manas.q: What are the two years of pre-primary called?

children.note: After PP2, children join Grade 1. KICD's 2019 framework says Grade 1 starts at about age 6.

manas.q: Which grade comes straight after PP2?

children.note: Pre-primary plus lower primary (Grades 1–3) together make the early years stage (Early Years Education).

manas.q: Which two levels make up Early Years Education?

children.note: The official pages we read do not give exact ages for PP1 and PP2. Ask your school or county about entry age.
Young children learn best by doing: playing, singing, building, drawing and talking. Pre-primary is built around this, not around long written work.

manas.q: What is the main way young children learn in pre-primary?

children.note: KICD's December 2024 list of approved materials names these learning areas for PP1 and PP2. Each one is taught through activities and play.
Listening, speaking, early reading and early writing, mostly through stories, songs and talk.

manas.q: Which pre-primary learning area covers listening, speaking and early reading?

children.note: Children listen to stories, follow simple instructions, answer questions and share their own news.
Children hear and say the sounds letters make, often with songs and actions, before reading words.
Holding a crayon, drawing lines and circles, tracing, then forming letters. Strong small finger muscles come first.
Early number work through counting, sorting and playing with real objects.

manas.q: Which learning area covers counting, sorting and shapes?

children.note: Counting bottle tops, stones, cups or children in a line, and matching number names to objects.
Grouping things by colour, size or shape, and making simple patterns like big–small–big–small.
Naming circles and squares, comparing long and short, heavy and light, full and empty.
Learning about the world around them: themselves, family, home, plants, animals, weather, and keeping clean and safe.

manas.q: Which learning area teaches about plants, animals, weather and keeping clean?

children.topic: Me, my body and my family
children.note: Naming body parts, family members and people who help us in the community.
Watching seeds grow, caring for plants, naming animals, and noticing sun and rain.
Washing hands, using the toilet properly, and simple safety at home and on the road.
Art, music, movement and play that build imagination and strong bodies.

manas.q: Which learning area includes art, music, movement and outdoor play?

children.note: Painting, colouring, tearing paper and modelling with clay or play dough.
Singing, clapping rhythms, dancing and simple drama or role play.
Outdoor play builds balance, coordination and big muscles (gross motor skills).
The 2024 list names Christian Religious Education and Islamic Religious Education for pre-primary. Families usually follow the option that matches their faith; check with your school.

manas.q: Which two religious education options are listed for pre-primary?

children.note: Simple Bible stories, songs and prayers, and learning to be kind and share.
Simple stories, short prayers and good manners taught in the Islamic tradition.
KICD's 2024 list shows Kiswahili materials for PP2. Children hear and use simple Kiswahili words, greetings, songs and stories.

manas.q: In which pre-primary year does KICD's 2024 list show Kiswahili?

children.note: The 2019 framework used slightly different names, such as Psychomotor and Creative Activities and Pre-Braille Activities. Current KICD lists use the names above.
A predictable day helps small children feel safe and ready to learn. Each school sets its own timetable.
A warm welcome, hanging up bags, and a short circle time with songs or news.
Lessons are short and active because young children cannot sit still for long.
Free play and games outside, which are learning time too, not just a break.
Children practise handwashing, eating tidily and using the toilet on their own.
Some schools have a short rest or quiet story time. Ask about your school's routine.
Regular times for sleep, meals and play at home make school mornings much easier.
The CBC names seven core competencies. In pre-primary they show up in very simple, everyday ways.
Taking turns, sharing toys, and telling others what they need in words.

manas.q: Which core competency covers taking turns and sharing?

children.note: Putting on shoes, packing a bag, trying again after a mistake.
Working out how to fit a puzzle piece or how to share three sweets fairly.
Playing shop, building with boxes, making up stories and songs.
Asking 'why?', exploring and wanting to find out more.
Values in the CBC include respect, responsibility, care and compassion, and honesty. Small children learn them by copying adults and by gentle praise.

manas.q: Name two CBC values a small child can practise every day.

children.note: At this age there are no big exams. Teachers mostly watch children as they play and work and keep simple records of progress.
Teachers notice what a child can do: hold a pencil, count to ten, join in a song. This is the main way young children are assessed.

manas.q: What is the main way teachers assess pre-primary children?

children.note: Teachers may tick off skills on a list or write short notes about each child. Methods vary by school.
Drawings, colouring and early writing may be kept in a folder to show growth over time.
Asking a child to tell about a picture or count objects shows what they understand.
Reports usually describe what the child can do and what to work on, not a mark or position. Ask your school how it reports.
Assessment here is to help each child grow, not to compare children with each other.
Children who hear lots of talk and stories find reading easier later. This costs almost nothing.
Chat while cooking, walking or shopping. Name things and ask 'what do you see?'

children.topic: Read or tell a story daily
children.note: Ten minutes a day is enough. Old stories from grandparents count too.

manas.q: How long a daily story time is enough to help early reading?

children.note: Rich talk in your home language helps a child learn English and Kiswahili later.
'I spy something that starts with mmm… maize!' Builds letter-sound skills.
Trace letters with a finger in sand, soil or flour on a tray.
Point to words on packets, matatus and shop signs and say them together.
Rhymes help children hear the sounds inside words.
Everyday life is full of maths. Use real things the child can touch.
Count tomatoes into the bag, or how many oranges you bought.
Count steps to the gate or while climbing stairs together.
Sort socks by colour, or spoons from forks. Sorting is early maths.
Collect bottle tops for counting, adding one more, and making patterns.
Find circles (plates), squares (windows) and triangles around the home.
Compare cups, sticks or shoes by size, length or weight.
One plate for each person teaches matching one-to-one.
Simple, low-cost activities that build hands, bodies and imagination.
Mix flour, salt, water and a little oil. Rolling and squeezing strengthens fingers for writing.

manas.q: Why is playing with dough good preparation for writing?

children.topic: Kitchen garden or seed in a tin
children.note: Plant beans in a tin and watch them grow. Talk about water and sun.
Old boxes and tins make towers, cars and houses.
Use empty packets and bottle tops as money to play buying and selling.
Throwing, catching, hopping and skipping build strong bodies.
Carrying a light basket, watering plants or folding cloths teaches responsibility.

children.topic: Draw with a stick in soil
children.note: No paper needed: draw shapes and lines on the ground outside.
Choose short, good-quality videos and watch together. Real play and talk matter more.
A healthy, well-rested, safe child learns better.
Young children need a lot of sleep. A regular bedtime helps them focus at school.
Simple foods like porridge, eggs, fruit or githeri give energy for learning.
Teach washing before eating and after the toilet. A tippy-tap at home works well.
Keep up with clinic check-ups and vaccinations as advised by your health worker.
Teach holding hands near roads, and keep medicines, sharp things and paraffin out of reach.
Teach the names of body parts and that they can tell you if anyone makes them feel uncomfortable.

children.topic: 💛 When a child needs extra help
children.note: Every child grows at their own pace. Some signs mean it is worth asking for a check, early and gently.
Not turning to sounds, holding things very close, or squinting a lot.
Very few words, or speech that close family cannot understand.
Often falling, or great difficulty holding a crayon or using a spoon.

children.topic: Very hard to settle or join in
children.note: Extreme distress every day for weeks, or rarely playing with others.
Teachers see many children and can share what they notice. Work together, without blame.
If worried, visit a clinic, paediatrician or a county assessment centre. Early help makes a big difference.

manas.q: If you are worried about a young child's development, what is a good next step?

children.note: Readiness is about independence and confidence, not just knowing letters and numbers.
Using the toilet, eating, dressing and packing a bag without much help.

manas.q: Name one sign of independence that helps a child get ready for Grade 1.

children.note: Listening and doing two-step tasks like 'get your bag and sit down'.

children.topic: Sitting and listening a bit longer
children.note: Being able to listen to a short story to the end.
Sharing, waiting a turn and asking for help politely.
Lower primary (Grade 1–3) adds learning areas such as English, Kiswahili and Mathematics. See the Lower primary map.
Talk positively about Grade 1 and, if possible, visit the classroom before the year starts.
